title: Ingredient Groups

examples.explanation: "abc" and "bca" are one mix, "aab" and "aba" are another, and "xyz" is on its own.
"abb" uses b twice, so it is a different mix from "ab" and "ba".

constraints: codes[i] contains only lowercase letters a-z

approaches.name: sorted letters as a key, counted in a set
26-letter count tuple as a key, counted in a set

steps.title: Clarify the input
steps.description: Confirms that letter counts matter, and asks what to do with an empty list, an empty code and repeated identical codes.
look_for: asks whether 'ab' and 'abb' are the same mix
hints: Before you start, is there anything about what makes two codes 'the same mix' that you'd want to confirm?
Would 'ab' and 'abb' be the same mix? What about two identical codes?
Settle letter counts, duplicates and empty inputs before you pick a data structure.

steps.title: Find a shared signature
steps.description: Realizes that codes in the same mix can be turned into one identical 'signature', for example by sorting their letters or counting each letter.
look_for: sorts the letters of each code
says codes in a group should map to the same key
hints: Think about what 'abc' and 'bca' have in common that 'abb' doesn't.
Could you rewrite each code into a form where all codes in the same mix look exactly alike?
Sorting a code's letters, or counting each letter, gives every code in a mix the same signature.

steps.title: Count distinct signatures
steps.description: Puts each signature into a set or dictionary and returns how many distinct signatures there are, instead of comparing every pair of codes.
look_for: returns the number of distinct keys
says comparing every pair would be too slow
hints: Look at how you're deciding whether a code belongs to a group you've already seen.
Once each code has a signature, what structure tells you quickly whether you've seen that signature before?
Store signatures in a hash set; the answer is how many distinct ones you end up with.

steps.title: Make the signature hashable
steps.description: Uses a signature type that can go into a set or be a dictionary key, such as a string or tuple rather than a list.
look_for: joins sorted letters into a string
mentions that lists can't be dictionary keys
hints: Check what type your signature is before you add it to the set.
Can every Python type be stored in a set?
Lists can't go into a set; turn the signature into a string or a tuple.

steps.title: Handle the edge inputs
steps.description: Returns 0 for an empty list, treats duplicates as one group, and treats the empty code as a mix of its own.
look_for: tests or mentions the empty list
tests or mentions an empty code
hints: Try your code on the smallest inputs you can think of.
What answer do you get for no codes at all, or for a code with no letters?
Make sure an empty list gives 0 and an empty code still counts as one group.

edge_cases.description: every code is a different mix
every code is the same mix

common_mistakes.description: uses the set of letters as the signature, which ignores how many times each letter appears
common_mistakes.symptom: puts 'ab' and 'abb' in the same group

common_mistakes.description: uses the sorted list of letters directly as a set element or dictionary key
compares every pair of codes and counts matches instead of groups
common_mistakes.symptom: returns the wrong count when a group has three or more codes, and is too slow for large inputs

wrap_up_questions: What are the time and space complexity?
How would you change this to return the groups themselves, and what if codes could be thousands of letters long?

origin_note: Original. Pattern: canonical signature counted in a hash set.
